wordsPreamble:
- English, with a Glasgow accent and a set of Scots words that visitors from England find harder than Edinburgh’s. People will slow down if you ask.
- Glasgow is famously open. Strangers start conversations at bus stops and in pub queues, and a short answer reads as unfriendly rather than polite.
- The humour is dry, quick and often at someone’s expense, including yours. Giving some back is expected.
- Football runs deep. Celtic and Rangers are a divide with religious and political history, so don’t pick a side casually or wear either strip into a pub.

words.context: Universal, at every age and in every setting. Aye, right — with the stress on right — means the opposite.
Also nae for “not” — nae bother means no problem.
A greeting, not a question. “No bad, yersel?” closes it. Awright? does the same job in one word.
Cheerio is still current. Shop staff often send you off with cheers, pal or cheers, hen — pal for men, hen for women.
Standard. Thanks very much is fine; ta is understood but sounds English.
Used freely. Sorry? also means “what did you say,” which you may need often.
Bar staff work out the order from who arrived when. A nod and eye contact are enough; waving money is not.

words.groupNote: Sorry covers both apology and getting past. Excuse me opens a request.

words.context: Or just name it — a pint of Tennent’s, please. Glasgow is not fussy about phrasing.
Asking for the check marks you instantly, though nobody will mind.
Sometimes added for groups and shown at the bottom of the bill. Otherwise tipping around 10% for table service is normal.
Tap a bank card on most city buses. The Subway is a single circular line, nicknamed the Clockwork Orange after its trains.
Loo works and the cludgie is old Glasgow slang for it. Restroom gets a blank look.

words.groupNote: Standard on most doors. Gaelic signs at stations use Fir for men and Mnathan for women.

words.context: Also the hole in the wall. Cash machines here dispense Scottish banknotes.
Contactless almost everywhere, including most chip shops and taxis.
Three Scottish banks print their own notes. They are legal across the UK but some English shops hesitate, so spend them here.
Charged. Doing the messages means doing the grocery shopping, so bring one if you are.
Glasgow’s favourite compliment for a person or a move with some swagger. Originally it meant fit for the gallows.
From wee ane, little one. The weans are the kids, and a greetin’ wean is a crying one.
Irn-Bru, cola, lemonade — all ginger in Glasgow. A bottle of ginger has nothing to do with ginger.
For a smell, a room, a pub toilet or the weather. Also used of a person who badly needs a wash.
One of many Glasgow words for it, alongside blootered and mortal. Usually said with some admiration.
